extracted.intended_audience: administrative law attorneys, agency policymakers, labor-law practitioners, and judges considering deference and rulemaking challenges
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether an agency regulation is within statutory delegation, reasonable, and entitled to judicial deference (Chevron/Auer/Mead), and whether notice-and-comment procedures satisfied APA 'fair notice' requirements. Applies to disputes about coverage under statutory exemptions (here, FLSA companionship-services exemption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency gap‑filling authority (Chevron)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s power to administer a congressionally created program necessarily requires the making of rules to fill any 'gap' left, implicitly or explicitly, by Congress; when an agency fills such a gap reasonably and in accordance with other applicable (e.g., procedural) requirements, that result is legally binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council: determine whether Congress spoke directly to the precise question; if not, ask whether the agency’s interpretation is a permissible construction of the statute. Consider whether the regulation is a reasonable answer to statutory ambiguities and whether procedural requirements were followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether regulation exceeds delegated rulemaking authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must assess whether the agency acted within the scope of definitional or other authority granted by Congress (e.g., the FLSA’s grant empowering DOL to define 'domestic service employment' and 'companionship services').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine statutory text and delegation (here, 1974 Amendments, §29(b)) to see if Congress left definitional gaps and empowered the agency to fill them; if the statute leaves questions open (who to include/exclude), rulemaking to resolve those details falls within delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness in light of agency expertise and policy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s choice resolving complex questions (e.g., whether to include all, some, or none of third‑party-paid workers) is reasonable when based on the agency’s expertise, knowledge of the area, and consultation with affected parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference is appropriate where satisfactory answers may turn upon agency expertise and consultation; courts should infer Congress intended such definitional authority where the agency is best positioned to resolve complex implementation questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity principle: more specific regulation governs in conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: When one regulation is specifically directed at the question at issue and another is more general, the more specific regulation governs (citing Morales v. Trans World Airlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two regulations appear to conflict, identify each regulation’s purpose: the one whose 'sole purpose' addresses the contested question should control; assess which provision is more specific regarding the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of agency interpretations of its own regulation (Auer-style acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may accept an agency’s interpretation of its own regulation where the agency’s course of action indicates the interpretation reflects its considered views and is not merely a post hoc rationalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the agency’s history of treatment of the regulation, whether the interpretation is advanced in a considered manner (e.g., advisory memorandum, notice-and-comment), and whether there is reason to suspect post hoc rationalization. An interpretation issued to agency personnel may be accepted when it fairly represents the agency’s considered position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors distinguishing interpretive rules from binding rules (Mead factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an agency action is a binding rule entitled to Chevron deference (rather than an interpretive statement) depends on factors such as whether it governs conduct of the public affecting individual rights and obligations, and whether the agency used notice-and-comment procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the rule 'affect[s] individual rights and obligations,' whether the agency used full public notice-and-comment procedures (not required for interpretive rules under 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(A)), and whether the rule falls within the statutory grant of authority and is reasonable. These indicators support treating the action as substantive and deserving deference (see United States v. Mead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of notice-and-comment: sufficiency and 'fair notice' (logical outgrowth)
rubrics_metrics.description: APA requires a notice of proposed rulemaking to contain either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved; courts generally require the final rule to be a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule so as to provide fair notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the final rule was reasonably foreseeable from the proposal; consider whether proposals considered (even if later withdrawn) gave sufficient notice that an alternative final approach was contemplated. A reasonably brief explanation for the final interpretation may suffice if it is consistent with the statutory language and no one objected at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement within regulatory subparts not dispositive but informative
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s placement of a regulation in an 'Interpretations' subpart versus a 'General Regulations' subpart is not controlling, but may indicate that the provision addresses matters of detail interpreting broader definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subpart placement as contextual evidence about the regulation’s character (detail/interpretation vs general definitional text), but do not treat placement alone as determinative of legal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding coverage anomalies and assessing practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing among competing readings of statutory/regulatory language, courts should consider whether adopting one interpretation would create serious problems or anomalies as to the coverage of particular employees or entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interpretations that avoid creating arbitrary or unworkable coverage gaps; consider historical coverage and administrative practicability when deciding which regulation governs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory memoranda and internal agency statements as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisory memoranda issued to agency personnel explaining a regulation can be accepted as reflecting the agency’s interpretation where the memorandum reflects the agency’s considered position and there is no reason to view it as post hoc rationalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such memoranda as persuasive evidence of the agency’s views when accompanied by consistent agency course of action and procedural formality (e.g., prior notice-and-comment and longstanding treatment). Absent such indicia, be cautious about relying on internal explanations.
